newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin marks 66th birthday weakened by ill health.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin marks 66th birthday weakened by ill health.

text.p: Boris Yeltsin celebrated his 66th birthday on Saturday weakened by ill health but the mayor of Moscow said the Russian president was alert, active and committed to returning to work.

"The president looked like anyone who had undergone a complicated heart operation and pneumonia, who is not fully fit," Interfax news agency quoted mayor Yuri Luzhkov as saying after visiting Yeltsin in the Gorki-9 residence outside Moscow.
"But the president is quite active and, judging by the speed of his mind and the depth of his thought, he is the same president we all used to know," Luzhkov added.

Yeltsin, who had undergone multiple bypass surgery in November and later suffered from heavy pneumonia, celebrated his birthday with his close family at Gorki-9 where he is convalescing after leaving hospital on January 20.
On Sunday Yeltsin will hold talks outside Moscow with French President Jacques Chirac, the first Western leader to see him since he was taken to hospital with pneumonia on January 8.
Doctors say he is recovering from the pneumonia.
But political opponents insist that the president, who had been away from office most of the time since he won a second term last July, is not at the helm.
They insist that Yeltsin should cede some of his sweeping powers or give them up altogether.
"The president is capable of working and the dreams of those who think that he may quit are nothing but fantasies," Luzhkov said.
Yeltsin himself on Friday rejected calls by political foes to amend the 1993 constitution to pass some of his powers to parliament and the government.
"The president cannot agree with such proposals," the Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky told a news briefing.
"In his opinion the constitution...has shown it can work, played and still plays an important stabilising role in society."

Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, who is due back in Russia on Saturday after taking part in the World Economic Forum in Switzerland, has said he plans to visit Yeltsin with a bouquet of flowers and a gift.
Brushing off charges that Yeltsin was unfit to rule, Chernomyrdin said his recovery would soon be evident.
"Soon there will be no basis for such speculation and such doubts. He's fully in control, political and state control and everybody will soon see that he's fit and able," he said.
Russian ultra-nationalist Vladimir Zhirinovsky sent his congratulations to Yeltsin promising his support for the ailing leader and urging him to take tougher anti-western and nationalist line.
"All sorts of impudent ethnic minorities are raising their heads while Russians are being humiliated and discriminated against," Interfax quoted Zhirinovsky's letter to Yeltsin as saying.
"Any state or foreign politician is welcome now to lecture Russia on what policy it should pursue, who to trade with, what to sell and what to buy."
